```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  comment = "#>",
  root.dir = './',
  eval = FALSE
)
```

This tutorial shows how to use tensor decomposition and module extraction on the fields the
previous tutorials produce: the field of every ligand-receptor pair is stacked into a
third-order tensor -- cells x components x LR pairs -- and factorised by CP (PARAFAC)
decomposition. The decomposition returns a set of components, each of which is a pattern of
LR-pair loadings; components whose loadings agree are then grouped into communication
modules, and every cell is scored against those modules.

Because a module is defined on the LR axis rather than on the cells, it is shared: the
same module can be scored in every sample of a study, which is what makes the module maps
of different samples comparable.

## About the data

The dataset behind this tutorial is not distributed. It is far too large to be shipped
through this channel, and it carries privacy and authorization constraints that neither
this tutorial nor this repository is in a position to take on. It starts from an expression
matrix imputed by an external tool, together with the cell metadata carrying the annotation
and the coordinates.

The chunks below are therefore shown rather than executed. They are the pipeline in the
order it runs, with the parameters it was run with, and every call in them is a function of
spWAVE -- none of it is pseudo-code. To run them on your own data, supply the field object
described in the next section.

## Setup

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)
library(parallel)

library(Seurat)
library(spWAVE)
```

## Compute the field of each sample

The pipeline starts from the object `perform_LR_field_hole_calc()` returns: cells
aggregated into meta-cells, and the field of every LR pair of the database estimated on
them. The [third tutorial](Field_est3.html) covers that step in detail; what matters here
is only what comes out of it, the `LR_pair_field` slot, an array of

```
cells  x  3  x  LR pairs        #  Ex, Ey, U
```

Samples are not listed by hand: the sample ids are read off the field objects present in
the data folder, so a sample is picked up by placing its files there.

```{r field objects}
#** folder holding the tutorial dataset, adjust it to your local copy
data_dir <- "../../data"

sample_ids <- sub(
  "_spwave_field\\.rds$", "",
  list.files(data_dir, pattern = "_spwave_field\\.rds$")
)
```

For reference, the per-sample half of the pipeline that produces those files is short --
the field estimation itself is the only expensive part, and it is the part the field
tutorials already walk through.

```{r field calculation}
lr_db <- load_database(db_source = "CellChat", db_species = "human")

#** the field of every LR pair is computed independently, so the work is spread over cores
future::plan("multicore", workers = 16)

for (id in sample_ids) {
  #** imputed expression, cells x genes, and the metadata holding x/y and the annotation
  imputed <- data.table::fread(
    file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_imputed.tsv")),
    sep = "\t", data.table = FALSE
  )
  rownames(imputed) <- imputed[, 1]
  imputed <- as.matrix(imputed[, -1])
  meta <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_meta.rds")))

  #** keep the cells the metadata describes, in its order
  cells   <- rownames(meta)
  imputed <- imputed[cells, , drop = FALSE]
  coord   <- data.frame(x = meta$x, y = meta$y, barcode = cells, row.names = cells)

  #** CreateSeuratObject() wants features x cells, hence the transpose
  srt <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = t(imputed), assay = "SCT", meta.data = meta)

  #** the metadata column holding the cell-type annotation is sample-specific
  cluster_colname <- "ct3"

  spwave <- create_spWAVE_object(
    seurat_obj = srt,
    database   = lr_db,
    cluster    = cluster_colname,
    coord      = coord
  )

  #** aggregating cells into meta-cells of about thirty cells each is what keeps the
  #** field estimation tractable on a large sample
  spwave <- generate_kmeans_coord(spwave, centers = ncol(srt) / 30,
                                  iter.max = 15, nstart = 3)
  spwave <- generate_meta_expr(spwave)
  spwave <- perform_LR_field_hole_calc(spwave)

  saveRDS(spwave, file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_spwave_field.rds")))
  rm(spwave, srt, meta, coord, imputed)
  gc()
}
```

## Build the tensor

`prep_TD_data()` turns that array into the tensor the decomposition runs on. It keeps two
of the three field components, and it keeps them on a log scale:

```{r tensor}
tnsr_list <- list()

for (id in sample_ids) {
  spwave <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_spwave_field.rds")))
  tnsr_list[[id]] <- prep_TD_data(spwave, low_quantile = 0.1)
}
```

What is left is

```
cells  x  2  x  LR pairs        #  logEx, logEy
```

The pair is not `Ex` and `Ey` but the **magnitude and the direction of the field, kept
apart**: the field strength goes into a log, and the direction is re-applied as a cosine
and a sine. Splitting them is what makes the tensor decomposable at all -- a raw `Ex` and
`Ey` mix strength and direction in the same number, so two cells with the same field
pointing in opposite directions look as different as two cells with different strengths.

`low_quantile` is the only other thing this step does: field magnitudes below the 10th
percentile of the sample are set to zero, so that the decomposition is not spent on
values that are numerically indistinguishable from noise.

## Align the LR axis across samples

The decomposition is run one sample at a time, but the samples cannot be treated in
complete isolation: their components are pooled in the next section, which only works if
every sample sits on the **same LR axis**. The tensor is therefore trimmed before anything
is decomposed.

```{r lr axis}
#** a pair is dropped when its maximum field magnitude is an outlier within a sample,
#** here beyond three standard deviations from the mean. the components of all samples
#** are pooled further down, which requires every sample to sit on one common LR axis,
#** so a pair that is an outlier in any sample is dropped from all of them
keep_lr <- dimnames(tnsr_list[[sample_ids[1]]])[[3]]

for (id in sample_ids) {
  lr_max  <- apply(tnsr_list[[id]], 3, function(x) max(abs(x)))
  lr_z    <- abs(lr_max - mean(lr_max)) / sd(lr_max)
  keep_lr <- intersect(keep_lr, names(lr_max)[lr_z <= 3])
}
```

## Run the CP decomposition

Each sample is decomposed on its own, over a range of ranks, several times per rank. The
decomposition is not deterministic -- the alternating least squares it runs converges to a
local optimum -- so what is kept is not one answer but a population of them: `num_rep`
accepted decompositions per rank, where a decomposition is accepted once its CORCONDIA
reaches `corcondia_cutoff`.

```{r cpd}
cl <- parallel::makeCluster(8, setup_strategy = "sequential")

CP_decomp_all <- list()

for (id in sample_ids) {
  tnsr_ft <- tnsr_list[[id]][, , keep_lr]
  saveRDS(tnsr_ft, file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_tensor.rds")))

  #** NOTE: the cache is only valid while keep_lr stays the same. adding or removing a
  #** sample can shrink keep_lr, which would mix decompositions computed on different
  #** LR axes, so clear the *_cp_decomp.rds files whenever the sample set changes
  cp_file <- file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_cp_decomp.rds"))

  if (file.exists(cp_file)) {
    CP_decomp <- readRDS(cp_file)
  } else {
    CP_decomp <- repeat_tensor_CPD(
      tensor           = tnsr_ft,
      num_rep          = 10,
      rank_range       = 10:15,
      const            = c("uncons", "uncons", "orthog"),
      corcondia_cutoff = 10,
      parallel         = TRUE,
      cl               = cl
    )
    saveRDS(CP_decomp, cp_file)
  }

  CP_decomp_all <- c(CP_decomp_all, unlist(CP_decomp, recursive = FALSE))
}
```

Three of those arguments carry the method:

- **`const`** sets one constraint per tensor mode. The cells are unconstrained, the two
  field components are unconstrained, and the **LR mode is orthogonal** -- the loadings of
  one component must be uncorrelated with those of the next, which is what makes a
  component readable as a set of LR pairs rather than as a mixture of all of them.
- **`rank_range = 10:15`** is a range rather than a rank because the right rank is not
  known in advance; the components of every rank are pooled, and the module clustering
  decides afterwards which of them describe the same thing.
- **`corcondia_cutoff = 10`** is the acceptance bar. CORCONDIA compares the fitted
  decomposition against the original tensor, and a decomposition below the cutoff is
  discarded rather than returned, up to `attempts` restarts.

The decompositions of a given rank are independent of each other, hence the cluster: this
is the expensive step of the whole tutorial, which is also why the result is cached per
sample.

## Correlate the components across samples

This is the part that runs **once, over every sample together**, unlike the two halves
around it. The LR-pair loadings of every component of every sample are correlated against
each other; two components are linked only where the correlation is strong and survives
multiple testing, and a component linked to too few others is dropped as an isolated one.

```{r correlation}
cor_mat_list <- construct_cor_mat(
  TD_result   = CP_decomp_all,
  R_cutoff    = 0.5,
  p_cutoff    = 0.05,
  link_cutoff = 10,
  return_raw  = TRUE
)
```

`R_cutoff` and `p_cutoff` are applied to the correlations and to their FDR-adjusted
p-values; `link_cutoff = 10` then removes the components left with ten or fewer links,
which is what keeps a component that agrees with nothing from becoming a module of its
own.

`return_raw = TRUE` returns both the filtered matrix and the unfiltered one. The
clustering uses the filtered matrix; the figure below uses the raw one, so that the
structure is not flattened by the threshold that was used to define it.

## Cluster the components into modules

```{r clustering}
module_list <- perform_dynamic_module_clustering(
  cor_mat        = cor_mat_list$cor_ft,
  linkage_method = "average",
  offset         = NULL,
  MIN_THRESHOLD  = 15,
  Z_THRESHOLD    = NULL
)

ft_names <- rownames(cor_mat_list$cor_ft)
ht <- plot_cor_module_heatmap(
  cor_mat     = cor_mat_list$cor_raw[ft_names, ft_names],
  module_list = module_list
)

pdf(file.path(data_dir, "module_cor_heatmap.pdf"), width = 8, height = 8)
ComplexHeatmap::draw(ht)
dev.off()
```

The components are hierarchically clustered on `1 - correlation`, and the tree is cut
dynamically rather than at a fixed height. Two arguments control that cut, and they pull
in opposite directions:

- **`MIN_THRESHOLD = 15`** is a size guarantee. Two subtrees of at least fifteen
  components are never merged into one another, however similar they look, so a module
  that has grown large cannot swallow the next one.
- **`Z_THRESHOLD`** is the strictness of the cut itself. Left at `NULL` it falls at the
  median of the dendrogram heights; a smaller value cuts higher and yields fewer, larger
  modules.

`plot_cor_module_heatmap()` draws the result, with the modules as an annotation bar. The
components that end up in no module are not an error: they are the ones the cut left
unassigned, and they stay out of the modules rather than being forced into one.

## Extract the LR pairs of each module

A module is a set of components, and each component is a set of LR-pair loadings. Turning
that into the LR pairs a module stands for means ranking the pairs within each of its
components and combining those rankings.

```{r module members}
#** any sample's tensor can be passed here: the function only reads its LR axis, and all
#** samples share the one defined above
module_LR_list <- extract_module_topLR(
  TD_result   = CP_decomp_all,
  tensor      = tnsr_list[[sample_ids[1]]][, , keep_lr],
  module_list = module_list,
  top_n       = 50
)
```

`top_n` is how many LR pairs are taken from each component before the rankings are
combined, so a module ends up holding the pairs that recur across the components assigned
to it rather than the pairs that happen to load highest in one of them.

```{r modules out}
saveRDS(
  list(
    cor_mat        = cor_mat_list,
    module_list    = module_list,
    module_LR_list = module_LR_list
  ),
  file.path(data_dir, "modules.rds")
)
```

This file is the shared half of the output: the module definition that every sample is
scored against, and therefore the one object a study has to keep.

## Score the cells

Scoring goes back to one sample at a time, but the modules stay shared, so the module
assignments of different samples are comparable.

```{r scoring}
rm(tnsr_list)
gc()

for (id in sample_ids) {
  tnsr_ft <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_tensor.rds")))

  #** ssGSEA of every module over the field magnitudes of that sample
  ssGSEA_scores <- scoring_cell_module(
    tensor         = tnsr_ft,
    module_LR_list = module_LR_list,
    BPPARAM        = BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(workers = 8, progressbar = TRUE),
    verbose        = TRUE
  )

  cell_assign <- assign_cell_module(
    ssGSEA_result     = ssGSEA_scores,
    score_cutoff      = 0.1,
    score_diff_cutoff = 0.03,
    min_cells         = 0.075 * ncol(ssGSEA_scores)
  )

  saveRDS(
    list(ssGSEA_scores = ssGSEA_scores, cell_assign = cell_assign),
    file.path(data_dir, paste0(id, "_cell_assign.rds"))
  )
}

parallel::stopCluster(cl)
```

The score of a cell on a module is an ssGSEA enrichment of that module's LR pairs over the
cell's field magnitudes -- the module is treated as a gene set and the field strength as
the quantity being enriched. It is a per-cell number, so the module of a cell is the one
it scores highest on.

Two corrections are applied on top of that, both aimed at the same failure mode: a cell
whose assignment is barely decided.

- **`score_cutoff = 0.1`** leaves a cell unassigned (`"other"`) when even its best score
  stays below it, rather than assigning it to whichever module happens to lead.
- **`score_diff_cutoff` and `min_cells`** act together. A module covering fewer than
  `min_cells` cells is a candidate for being absorbed, and a cell of such a module moves
  to its runner-up module when the two scores are within `score_diff_cutoff` of each
  other. A cell that is clearly its module's, or that belongs to a module of a reasonable
  size, keeps its assignment.

## Outputs

Per sample, `{sample}_cell_assign.rds` holds the ssGSEA scores of every cell against every
module and the resulting per-cell module assignment, which is what the spatial module maps
are drawn from: one map per module, coloured by the cells assigned to it.
